scenes.text: Some of the tallest dams in the world are thinner than you would believe. A wall of concrete can hold back a lake billions of tonnes heavy, while being only a few meters thick at the top. The secret is the curve. Bend a dam the right way, and the water pushes it tighter against the mountains instead of knocking it over. Today, eleven parts of a dam, and why each one exists.
scenes.caption: WHY IS IT CURVED?

scenes.text: Dams hold back rivers for drinking water, farms, flood control and electricity. Behind each one sits a huge weight of water, pressing harder the deeper it gets. If a big dam fails, the flood downstream can be one of the deadliest disasters humans can cause. So every part of a dam exists for a reason.
scenes.caption: A LAKE ON YOUR SHOULDERS

scenes.text: As always, every fact comes from a named source, dam operators, government agencies, and official investigation reports, all listed in the description. Let's start with the curve.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS EXIST?

scenes.text: Why are so many dams curved, with the bulge pointing toward the lake? Because the curve turns the push of the water into squeezing. A straight wall would be bent by the water like a ruler. An arch, curved upstream, sends that force sideways along the curve into the rock walls of the canyon. Concrete is very strong when squeezed, so the arch can be surprisingly thin.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS DAM CURVED?

scenes.text: It is the same idea as a stone arch in an old bridge or church. Push on the outside of an arch, and every block is pressed against its neighbors, holding the whole shape together. An arch dam is just an arch lying on its side, with the canyon walls as its supports.
scenes.caption: AN ARCH ON ITS SIDE

scenes.text: That is why arch dams are built in narrow canyons with strong rock, like the Contra Dam in Switzerland, two hundred and twenty meters tall, where James Bond made his famous bungee jump in GoldenEye. In a wide valley with weak rock, the arch would have nothing solid to push against.
scenes.caption: THE BOND JUMP

scenes.text: Why are some dams straight and enormously thick instead of curved and thin? Because they use a different trick, weight. A gravity dam simply stands in the way of the water and is so heavy that the water cannot push it over or slide it along the ground. It is shaped like a triangle, thin at the top and very wide at the base, where the water pressure is greatest.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS DAM SO THICK?
scenes.short: Why Are Some Dams So Thick?

scenes.text: Gravity dams work in wide valleys where an arch would not fit. China's Three Gorges Dam is one, more than two kilometers long and about one hundred and eighty meters tall, built with tens of millions of cubic meters of concrete. It is also the largest power station on Earth.
scenes.caption: TWO KILOMETERS LONG

scenes.text: Many dams combine both ideas. Hoover Dam, on the Colorado River, is an arch gravity dam. It is curved, so part of the water's force goes into the canyon walls, and it is very thick, about two hundred meters at the base, so its weight holds the rest.
scenes.caption: BOTH AT ONCE

scenes.text: Why is Hoover Dam full of pipes buried in its concrete? Because concrete gets hot as it hardens. The chemical reaction between cement and water releases heat. In a small slab, that heat escapes quickly. But engineers calculated that if Hoover Dam had been poured as one solid block, it would have taken more than a hundred years to cool down, and it would have cracked as it shrank.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE PIPES INSIDE THIS DAM?
scenes.chapter: 3. The pipes hidden in the concrete
scenes.short: Why Was Hoover Dam Built With Pipes Inside?
scenes.file: File:"Ready for a concrete pour in block 14G, showing cleaned bedrock and form work on which are mounted the metal... - NARA - 294147.jpg

scenes.text: So the dam was built as many separate columns, poured in blocks, with about a thousand kilometers of steel pipes inside. River water and then chilled water from a refrigeration plant was pumped through the pipes, cooling the concrete in months instead of a century. Afterwards, the pipes were filled with grout.
scenes.caption: A THOUSAND KILOMETERS OF PIPE

scenes.text: The same problem exists in every big concrete pour today. Large dams, bridge foundations and building cores are still cooled with pipes, ice in the mix, or poured in layers. Hidden inside, a dam is as much a cooling system as a wall.
scenes.caption: A WALL THAT HAD TO COOL

scenes.text: Why does a dam have a huge concrete channel down its side, like a water slide? Because the most dangerous thing for a dam is water going over the top where it should not. In a big flood, the lake fills faster than the turbines can use it. The spillway lets the extra water out safely, around or over the dam, without washing away its foundations.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS DAM HAVE A GIANT SLIDE?
scenes.short: Why Do Dams Have a Giant Concrete Slide?

scenes.text: For an earth dam, made of soil and rock, water flowing over the top is fatal. It erodes the dam from the top down within hours. So spillways are designed for floods far bigger than any recorded, sometimes the largest flood thought possible at that river.
scenes.caption: THE BIGGEST FLOOD POSSIBLE

scenes.text: In February two thousand seventeen, the main spillway of California's Oroville Dam, the tallest dam in the United States, broke apart during heavy rains. Water then began flowing down the emergency spillway, which started eroding. Nearly two hundred thousand people were evacuated. The dam held, but the spillway had to be rebuilt.
scenes.caption: OROVILLE, 2017

scenes.text: Why do some spillway tunnels have slots that suck air into the water? Because fast water can eat concrete. When water flows very fast over a small bump, the pressure drops so low that tiny bubbles of vapor form, and then collapse violently. This is called cavitation. Each collapse is a tiny hammer blow, and millions of them can tear holes in solid concrete.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS SPILLWAY NEED AIR?
scenes.chapter: 5. The air slots in the tunnel
scenes.short: Why Do Dam Spillways Need Air Holes?

scenes.text: In nineteen eighty three, a huge snowmelt flood forced Glen Canyon Dam, in Arizona, to use its spillway tunnels for weeks. Cavitation tore out concrete, steel and even rock, and the tunnels shook and spat out debris. Workers even added plywood boards on top of the spillway gates to hold back a little more water.
scenes.caption: GLEN CANYON, 1983

scenes.text: After the flood, engineers added aeration slots. Air mixed into the water acts as a cushion, so the collapsing bubbles cannot hit the concrete so hard. It is an elegant fix. To protect the tunnel from water, you let air in.
scenes.caption: AIR AS A CUSHION

scenes.text: Why are there tall towers standing in the lake in front of Hoover Dam? They are intake towers. They let water into the dam's power plant, through gates at different heights. Taking water from the right depth matters. Water near the bottom may be colder and carry more silt, while water near the surface may be warmer.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE TOWERS IN THIS LAKE?
scenes.short: Why Are There Towers Standing in Front of Hoover Dam?
scenes.file: File:Water intake towers and Hoover Dam.jpg

scenes.text: Hoover Dam has four of these towers, each one taller than a twenty five story building, with huge cylinder gates that can be opened or closed. Water flows from them through tunnels in the canyon walls to the turbines below. Screens on the towers stop logs and debris from going in.
scenes.caption: FOUR TOWERS

scenes.text: Many dams have intake structures like these, but few are as beautiful. Hoover Dam was built in the nineteen thirties with art deco details, and even its clocks on the towers show two different times. One for Nevada and one for Arizona, the two states on either side of the dam.
scenes.caption: TWO TIME ZONES

scenes.text: Why are the pipes that carry water to a dam's turbines so huge? They are called penstocks, and they have to carry enormous amounts of water under high pressure. At Hoover Dam, the main penstocks are about nine meters across, big enough to drive a truck through. The bigger the pipe, the slower the water flows for the same amount, and the less energy is lost to friction.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THESE PIPES SO HUGE?
scenes.short: Why Are Dam Pipes Big Enough to Drive Through?

scenes.text: The weight of the lake behind the dam is what makes the electricity. The deeper the turbines sit below the surface, the more pressure pushes the water through them. At the bottom, the water spins the turbines, which turn generators, and then flows out into the river below.
scenes.caption: THE WEIGHT MAKES POWER

scenes.text: Closing a penstock gate suddenly would be dangerous. All that moving water would slam to a stop, creating a pressure shock called water hammer, strong enough to burst the pipe. So gates close slowly, and many plants have surge tanks that let the water rise and fall to absorb the shock.
scenes.caption: WATER HAMMER

scenes.text: Why are there tunnels running through the inside of a concrete dam? They are inspection galleries. Engineers walk through them to check the dam from the inside. They measure cracks, temperature, movement, and especially water that seeps through the concrete and the rock below. A dam is not supposed to be perfectly watertight, but leaks must be watched.
scenes.caption: WHY ARE THERE TUNNELS INSIDE THIS DAM?
scenes.short: Why Are There Tunnels Inside a Dam?
scenes.file: File:Inspection gallery beneath Roadford Dam - geograph.org.uk - 3653589.jpg

scenes.text: Water seeping under a dam can push upward on it, like the dam is trying to float. This is called uplift, and it reduces the dam's grip on the ground. So drains are drilled from the galleries into the rock below, letting that water escape and lowering the pressure.
scenes.caption: THE DAM TRIES TO FLOAT

scenes.text: Inside many dams, there are also hanging wires called plumb lines, which show if the dam leans a few millimeters more in summer or under a full lake. Big dams bend a little with the water level and the temperature, and engineers have records of those movements going back decades.
scenes.caption: PLUMB LINES

scenes.text: Why do some dams have a staircase of small pools beside them? It is a fish ladder. Salmon and other fish swim upstream to lay their eggs where they were born. A dam blocks their path completely. A fish ladder gives them a route of small steps, each one a pool, that they can jump or swim up, one level at a time.
scenes.caption: WHY DOES THIS DAM HAVE STAIRS FOR FISH?
scenes.short: Why Do Some Dams Have Stairs for Fish?
scenes.file: File:Fish ladder at Kerkhove weir, Avelgem, 2026.jpg

scenes.text: On the Columbia River, in the United States, big dams like Bonneville have fish ladders with windows where visitors can watch salmon pass and staff count them. Some dams even use fish elevators, or trucks, to carry fish over the wall.
scenes.caption: COUNTING SALMON

scenes.text: Getting young fish back downstream is just as hard, because the turbines and spillways can hurt them. So modern dams use screens, bypass channels, and fish friendly turbines. A dam is not just a wall for water. It is a wall in the middle of an ecosystem.
scenes.caption: A WALL IN AN ECOSYSTEM

scenes.text: Why is the Vajont Dam in Italy still standing, even though nearly two thousand people died below it? Because the dam did not fail. In October nineteen sixty three, a huge landslide, more than two hundred and fifty million cubic meters of rock, slid from a mountain into the lake behind it. It pushed a wave of water over the top of the dam.
scenes.caption: WHY DID THIS DAM SURVIVE BUT THE TOWN DIE?
scenes.chapter: 10. The mountain that fell into the lake
scenes.short: Why Did This Dam Survive but the Town Below Didn't?
scenes.file: File:Diga del Vajont vista da Erto.jpg

scenes.text: The wave rose far above the dam and fell into the narrow valley below, destroying the town of Longarone and nearby villages in minutes. The dam, a thin arch, was barely damaged. Warning signs of the moving mountain had been seen for years, and the investigation found that the risk had been underestimated.
scenes.caption: LONGARONE, 1963

scenes.text: Vajont changed dam engineering forever. Engineers now study the whole valley, not just the dam. The slopes around the lake, the geology, and how the rock behaves when the water rises and falls. The strongest dam in the world is useless if the mountain next to it is not stable.
scenes.caption: STUDY THE WHOLE VALLEY

scenes.text: Why is the Itaipu Dam split exactly between Brazil and Paraguay? Because it sits on the Parana River, the border between them. The two countries built it together and own it fifty fifty. It has twenty generating units, half of them running on Brazil's electrical frequency and half on Paraguay's.
scenes.caption: WHY IS THIS DAM SPLIT BETWEEN 2 COUNTRIES?
scenes.chapter: 11. The dam shared by two countries
scenes.short: Why Is This Giant Dam Split Between Two Countries?

scenes.text: Brazil uses sixty hertz electricity and Paraguay uses fifty, so the two halves of the plant produce power at different frequencies. Paraguay uses only a part of its share and sells most of the rest to Brazil. For years, Itaipu produced more electricity in a single year than any other plant on Earth.
scenes.caption: 50 AND 60 HERTZ

scenes.text: It shows that a dam is not only an engineering problem. It is a political one, a legal one, and a human one. Every curve, pipe and tunnel you have seen today exists because a whole country is downstream, trusting that the wall will hold.
scenes.caption: A COUNTRY DOWNSTREAM

scenes.text: So here are the eleven. A curve that squeezes instead of bends, and a thick wall that wins by weight. Pipes that cooled the concrete, a giant slide for floods, and air slots that stop the water eating the tunnels. Towers in the lake, pipes big enough to drive through, tunnels inside the dam, stairs for fish, a mountain that fell into the lake, and a dam shared by two countries.
scenes.caption: 11 PARTS. BILLIONS OF TONNES.

scenes.text: Next time you see a dam, look at its shape, and you will know which trick it uses to hold the water back. If you want more machines and structures explained part by part, subscribe to Machine Reverse. And tell us in the comments what you want us to take apart next.
scenes.caption: SUBSCRIBE: MACHINE REVERSE
